newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND-Poll points to strong Far East stocks gain.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Poll points to strong Far East stocks gain.

text.p: Equities investors should steer clear of the United States and look to the Far East and "Club Med" countries for the best returns in 1997, according to a Reuters poll of analysts published on Wednesday.

While the United States and some European bourses would struggle to maintain the dizzy returns of 1996, Italy, Spain, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan and South Africa could each swell by more than 14 percent from current levels in the coming year.
Reuters surveyed 137 analysts in 14 countries between December 3 and 10 for their 1997 year-end projections for the world's top 15 bourses by market capitalisation.

The fortunes of the major stock markets in New York, Tokyo and London will be mixed in 1997, with the chances of higher U.S. interest rates pushing the Dow Jones and Nasdaq composite indices lower. Both are forecast to dip by around six percent to around 6,060 points and 1,230 points respectively by end-1997.
The U.S. market soared more 28 percent in the last year and strategists have warned of a major correction.
"I think we've overdone it. "We're going into a big corrective phase and it's going to last a long time," said Alan Newman, technical market analyst at H.D. Brous & Co.
"I think it will be a tough year, down early and staying there for most of 1997," agreed Robert Dickey, chief technical analyst at Dain Bosworth in Minneapolis.
London's FTSE-100 index was expected to fare better, although not repeating this year's gains.

The FTSE is expected to rise by five percent from current levels to end 1997 at around 4,250. It has climbed nine percent so far this year, but political woes and the prospect of an interest rate hike have subdued market sentiment.

"It is difficult to talk about positive factors in an election year in the U.K. But the economy is showing very robust growth. We've got about 3.7 percent GDP growth next year, which we think will translate into good corporate profits growth," said Gary Dugan, European equity market strategist at JP Morgan.
The left-of-centre opposition Labour party are opinion poll favourites to win the next election, but a Labour victory would not send stocks into the doldrums, analysts said.

Japan's Nikkei 225 index looks the best bet out of the three top indices. Brokers are taking a bullish stance, with government efforts to promote deregulation and administrative reforms likely to boost stocks to around 23,500 by the end of the year, marginally higher than the 1996 high of 22,750.7 reached on June 24, but 14 percent higher than current levels.
Bourses in Canada, Switzerland and Australia would see growth of around eight percent. But rises in the German, French and Dutch stock markets would be more sluggish.

Falling interest rates should encourage higher returns in Italy and Spain where the major indices are each expected to grow by 15 percent. Both countries are undergoing stringent budgetary measures in order to meet the Maastricht criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

The BCI or Comit index in Italy would end 1997 at around 645 points, the survey showed, while Spain's IBEX-35 could reach around 5,490 points. It closed at 4,753.18 on December 10, after retreating during the day from an all-time high of 4,760.08.
Hong Kong's mid-year handover to China from British rule should not unsettle, and may in fact buoy the Far Eastern markets, strategists said.

"The China factor has been turning more positive and mainland funds are coming to Hong Kong buying property and equities. There are signs that more will be coming," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International in Hong Kong.
The Hang Seng Index, which closed at 13,149 on December 11 is expected to reach around 15,270 -- up around 16 percent.
In Taiwan too, the TAIEX should reap the benefits of a bullish 'Greater China' market.

South Africa's all-share index could surge almost 16 percent to around 7,700 points, prompted by growing world economies and substantial earnings growth. It closed at 6,666.4 on December 10, well off an all-time high of 7,099.4 on October 15.

Canadian stocks may reap the benfits from poor Dow and Nasdaq performances, with wary investors tempted to switch funds north of the border. That should offset any dampening effects from the fear of Canadian interest rate rises, strategists said.
They predicted the Toronto stock exchange's 300 composite index would rise to around 6,470 by the end of 1997 -- a surge of around nine percent on current levels.

Swiss indices are set for a year of steady growth, with the blue-chip Swiss Market Index putting on seven percent to end 1997 at 4,155 points, and the all-share Swiss Performance index ending up eight percent at 2,680 points.

In Australia, the All Ordinaries index should grow by around eight percent to end 1997 at around 2,540 points, the survey showed, with stong earnings growth offsetting any downward pressure from the U.S. correction.
In Europe, worries over meeting the Maastricht EMU criteria would keep the lid on German, French and Dutch exchanges.
France's CAC 40 should show around seven percent growth to end the year at 2,400 points. It hit a 1996 high of 2,358.65 on December 3.

In Germany, the DAX 30 would climb to 3,070 points -- a growth rate of six percent from current levels, and the AEX in the Netherlands would plod up 645 points, representing a three percent growth rate.
